I think ultimately the fix in Afghanistan is going to be a negotiated solution. getting the Taliban to the table under the right conditions and you know whether it's integrating some aspect of them into government or giving them a voice or you know not doing it but ceasing the war uh... but the second you put a timeline on actual military troops there uh... you give them a horizon to look at and a good friend of mine michael waltz he wrote a book about his time in afghanistan he's a uh... green berry officer he said literally the day that announcement came out he had been you know in these sessions with the village elders I forget what they're called but he said after that announcement they quit meeting with him and they said simply look we love you guys but you're leaving and now we have to think about that in the long term so yeah again it's it's not a decision I think anybody made out of a bad place but I think when you put timelines down against a really determined enemy you know that that's not good at the same token we have to understand no war has ended that I know of you know well with the exception of where countries totally destroyed without some version of a negotiated end My last question for you is about exactly that. Like you said, wars end when people make a decision to end them. It's very rare that there's some sort of, you know, you wipe out the entire enemy or there's some unilateral disarmament. Part of that's going to involve negotiations. It's going to be a negotiation between the United States, the Afghans, maybe the Pakistanis and the Taliban. I saw firsthand how hard it is to do something that complicated with US politics looming all over it. Specifically, it came with a guy named Bo Bergdahl who went AWOL in Afghanistan, was held by the Taliban for five years, and getting him back was a priority in and of itself, but it became part of a process where we were talking to the Afghans about essentially sending them doing a prisoner exchange where five decrepit old Taliban creeps down in Gitmo got sent back. They gave us bow and it was sort of seen as a confidence building measure that would help us get to a negotiated solution or build confidence or allow like more important talks that go on. That decision became one of the most quickly politicized things that I have ever seen. So I guess the question is, how do we do something really hard and complicated in the context of US politics where everything will be politicized? yeah and you know what that's a really good question and a really good point and that's where i think what leadership on especially on issues of foreign policy is so important americans typically follow what the leader articulates out as an objective and whether it's president obama president trump or whoever comes next uh... when this war in the land someday uh... when this war ends in afghanistan it's going to take a leader articulating what the in-game strategy is for the domestic politics and i think you know when it comes to uh... how does this war in some day i think you have to have a stable estate more stable you have completely stable more stable afghan government uh... you know one thing people forget is something like eighty percent of the people of afghanistan want us to be there they believe in the partnership with america so i think once you get that to stability Once you get Pakistan to wherever you need them, we saw promising signs with them rescuing the family. I think then we can begin. You probably won't do this publicly. It'll be in secret to have negotiations with the Taliban to see where an end is. The worry, though, is if you enter negotiations from a point of weakness, you're, I think at that point, not going to have a successful conclusion or at least one that we'd like to see. Right. Congress, because you're great. Thank you so much. You bet. Thanks a lot. Thanks again to Congressman Kinsinger for being on the show. If you want to learn more about any of the things we talked about, check out the PODSAVE World Facebook page or follow me on Twitter at at TB2R08.
